title_eng: Detection of Hemiplegic Gait Using 6-axis Inertial Sensor
title_kor: Detection of Hemiplegic Gait Using 6-axis Inertial Sensor
abstract:
Abstract— In this research, we investigate the feasibility of 
hemiplegic gait detection using 3-axis acceleration and 3-axis 
angular rate measured with wearable inertial sensor. Forty-six 
and eight 6-axis inertial signals were recorded from 19 
hemiplegia patient and 4 normal participants, respectively. To 
classify the gait pattern, we applied random forest classifier, and 
mean and standard deviation of each axis is used as a classifier 
input attributes. In the result, the total accuracy of analysis was 
96.3%, and sensitivity was 75.0% and 100% for normal and 
hemiplegic gait, respectively. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Paralysis with hemiplegia after stroke is primarily caused 
by damage of the nervous system. However, after the primary 
injury, musculoskeletal flexibility decreases and muscle 
strength weakens chronically, thus it is essential to manage the 
severity through continuous rehabilitation. Severity of 
paralysis has been manually evaluated through MMT (manual 
muscle test) and MAS (modified ashworh scale) [1]. 
This study is a preliminary on the measurement and 
diagnosis technology for the automatic diagnosis of 
hemiplegia. It aims to distinguish between hemiplegic gait and 
normal gait using wearable inertial measurement devices and 
pattern classification algorithm. These automatic diagnostic 
techniques could be applied to diagnose hemiplegia severity, 
which has been evaluated only by a professional evaluator, and 
to predict hemiparesis risk.

mean and standard deviation of each axis is used as a classifier 
input attributes. In the result, the total accuracy of analysis was 
96.3%, and sensitivity was 75.0% and 100% for normal and 
hemiplegic gait, respectively. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Paralysis with hemiplegia after stroke is primarily caused 
by damage of the nervous system. However, after the primary 
injury, musculoskeletal flexibility decreases and muscle 
strength weakens chronically, thus it is essential to manage the 
severity through continuous rehabilitation. Severity of 
paralysis has been manually evaluated through MMT (manual 
muscle test) and MAS (modified ashworh scale) [1]. 
This study is a preliminary on the measurement and 
diagnosis technology for the automatic diagnosis of 
hemiplegia. It aims to distinguish between hemiplegic gait and 
normal gait using wearable inertial measurement devices and 
pattern classification algorithm. These automatic diagnostic 
techniques could be applied to diagnose hemiplegia severity, 
which has been evaluated only by a professional evaluator, and 
to predict hemiparesis risk. 
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS 
Twenty-three subjects (19 hemiplegia and 4 normal) were 
participated to experiment. Detail information of subject is 
described in Table 1. For data acquisition, we developed signal 
acquisition module that includes 6-axis inertia sensor and 
wireless communication. Signal acquisition module is located 
on lumbar using stretchable waist belt. (see Fig. 1) Measured 
6-axis inertial signals were transferred to laptop via Bluetooth 
communication. Signal of each axis was sampled 128 Hz. 
There are several known characteristics of hemiplegic gait 
such as left/right balance or walking speed, and these could be 
presented in inertial signal of gait. Therefore, we selected 12 
features from inertial signal; mean and standard deviation of 
each x-, y- and z-axis acceleration and angular rate. Then, we 
used random forests, an ensemble learning method that 
operate by constructing a multitude of decision trees, for 
learning and classification [2]. In validation process, we 
divided the class into two groups; hemiplegia and normal and 
used a 10-fold validation. We used Matlab 2016b (Mathworks, 
Inc., MA, USA) for signal processing and Weka 3.9.0, open 
source data mining software, for classification and validation. 
III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS 
Table 2 represents the confusion matrix of classification 
result. Result shows that every hemiplegia gait successfully 
classified, however, 2 of normal gait were misclassified as a 
hemiplegic gait. Overall classification accuracy was 96.3% 
(52/54). This result may seem as an acceptable level in 
detecting hemiplegic gait. However, it is not clear what factor 
have had a major effect. For example, age difference between 
groups might be a critical factor in distinguishing gaits. 
IV. CONCLUSION 
The results suggest that a wearable hemi paresis gait 
detection system has a possibility. For more reliable result, 
additional experiment and optimization will be conducted. 
REFERENCES 
[1] D. T. Wade, "Measurement in neurological rehabilitation," Current 
Opinion in Neurology, vol. 5, no. 5, pp. 682-686, 1992. 
[2] L. Breiman, "Random forests," Machine learning, vol. 45, no. 1, pp. 
5-32, 2001.
